## Proof

Let $n>1$ be odd. Define

$$a \;=\; \prod_{\substack{1\le i\le n\\ \gcd(i,n)=1}} i \pmod n.$$

The integers $i$ with $\gcd(i,n)=1$ are precisely the elements of the multiplicative group $G=(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^{\times}$. So $a$ is the product of all elements of $G$.

**Step 1: Reduce to involutions.** In any finite abelian group, pair each element $g$ with its inverse $g^{-1}$. When $g\neq g^{-1}$, the pair contributes $g\cdot g^{-1}=1$ to the product. Hence the total product equals the product of those elements satisfying $g=g^{-1}$, i.e. $g^{2}=1$. Thus

$$a \;\equiv\; \prod_{\substack{x\bmod n\\ x^{2}\equiv 1\pmod n}} x \pmod n.$$

**Step 2: Count the solutions of $x^{2}\equiv 1\pmod n$.** Write the prime factorization $n=\prod_{j=1}^{r} p_j^{e_j}$ (all $p_j$ odd, since $n$ is odd). By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, solving $x^{2}\equiv 1\pmod n$ is equivalent to solving $x^{2}\equiv 1\pmod{p_j^{e_j}}$ independently for each $j$.

For an odd prime power $p^{e}$, the congruence $x^{2}\equiv 1\pmod{p^{e}}$ has exactly two solutions, $x\equiv \pm 1\pmod{p^{e}}$ (since $p^{e}\mid (x-1)(x+1)$ and $\gcd(x-1,x+1)\mid 2$, coprime to $p$). Therefore the full solution set modulo $n$ has $2^{r}$ elements, one for each choice of signs $(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_r)\in\{\pm1\}^{r}$.

**Step 3: Compute the product of all solutions.** Under CRT the product of all $2^{r}$ solutions is computed coordinate-wise. For the $j$-th coordinate, fixing the other $r-1$ signs (giving $2^{r-1}$ choices) lets $\varepsilon_j$ run through $\{+1,-1\}$, contributing $(+1)(-1)=-1$ per choice. Hence the $j$-th coordinate of the total product is

$$(-1)^{\,2^{r-1}}.$$

- If $r=1$: $(-1)^{1}=-1$, so $a\equiv -1\pmod n$, i.e. $a=n-1$.
- If $r\ge 2$: $2^{r-1}$ is even, so $(-1)^{2^{r-1}}=1$ in every coordinate, giving $a\equiv 1\pmod n$.

**Step 4: Interpret in terms of $n$.** Since $n$ is odd and $>1$, $r=1$ means $n$ is a power of a single odd prime, $n=p^{k}$. The case $r\ge 2$ means $n$ has at least two distinct prime factors.

**Conclusion.**

$$\boxed{\;a \;=\; \begin{cases} n-1, & \text{if } n=p^{k}\text{ for some odd prime }p\text{ and }k\ge 1,\\[4pt] 1, & \text{if } n\text{ has at least two distinct prime factors.} \end{cases}\;}$$

Equivalently: $a\equiv -1\pmod n$ exactly when $(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^{\times}$ is cyclic (which for odd $n>1$ occurs precisely for prime powers), and $a\equiv 1\pmod n$ otherwise. This is Gauss's generalization of Wilson's theorem.
